overview.text: Boudicca was queen of the Iceni, a people of eastern Britain, during the early Roman occupation. Her husband Prasutagus had ruled as an ally of Rome. After he died, Roman authorities tried to take Iceni land, and Boudicca led a large revolt around AD 60–61. Her forces destroyed Roman settlements at Colchester, London, and St Albans before a Roman army defeated them. The uprising showed that conquest had not ended resistance to Roman rule. Boudicca died soon after the defeat. She remains a symbol of resistance in British history.

overview.text: The Belt and Road Initiative is a Chinese-led program of overseas infrastructure, trade, and investment launched under Xi Jinping in 2013. Its name joins a proposed overland Silk Road Economic Belt with a Maritime Silk Road linking ports and coastal routes. Projects and corridors may include railways, roads, ports, and energy infrastructure rather than one continuous route. The initiative aims to connect economies across Asia and beyond, but its effects depend on how individual projects are financed and managed. World Bank research identifies possible gains in trade and connectivity alongside risks involving debt, environmental damage, corruption, and weak transparency.

key_facts.text: Xi Jinping launched the initiative in 2013.
The Belt is overland; the Road refers to maritime connections.
Projects include roads, railways, pipelines, and ports.

overview.text: The Abbasid Caliphate replaced the Umayyad dynasty in 750 and shifted the center of Islamic political life eastward toward Iraq. The Abbasids founded Baghdad as their capital in 762; its trade, scholarship, and art made it a major city of the medieval Islamic world. Astronomers there studied and translated earlier Greek, Indian, and Iranian learning while developing new methods. The court later used Samarra as a capital for several decades. From the tenth century, regional dynasties reduced the caliphs’ direct political power. Mongol forces sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending Abbasid rule there, although later Abbasid claimants held largely symbolic positions in Egypt.

overview.text: The Battle of Bosworth Field was fought in Leicestershire on 22 August 1485 during the Wars of the Roses. Henry Tudor challenged King Richard III, whose army was larger. The Stanley forces waited before supporting Henry, helping turn the battle against Richard. Richard was killed in the fighting, and Henry became Henry VII, the first Tudor king. Bosworth is often treated as the decisive battle of the dynastic struggle between Lancaster and York, although fighting connected with the conflict continued afterward. Archaeological work has revised the battlefield’s location from an older identification centered on Ambion Hill, showing how physical evidence can reshape historical accounts.

Henry Tudor defeated Richard III and became Henry VII.
Richard III was the last English king killed in battle.

overview.text: Hannibal Barca was a Carthaginian commander in the Second Punic War against Rome. In 218 BCE he led an army from Spain across the Pyrenees and Alps into Italy, bringing war elephants on the difficult journey. This unexpected route made him one of antiquity’s best-known generals. Hannibal won major victories in Italy, including at Cannae in 216 BCE, but he did not win the war. The Roman commander Scipio Africanus defeated his forces at Zama in North Africa in 202 BCE. Hannibal’s campaigns are studied for their daring movement, battlefield tactics, and the challenge they posed to Roman power.

overview.text: Romania is a country in southeastern Europe whose capital is Bucharest and whose official language is Romanian. Its modern state grew from the union of Moldavia and Wallachia in the nineteenth century; international treaties recognized independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1878. A revolution in December 1989 ended the country’s communist regime. Romania joined the European Union in 2007, and its currency remains the Romanian leu. Its political system has both a president as head of state and a prime minister as head of government. These institutions and dates help distinguish the modern country from the older principalities that preceded it.

overview.text: Phoenician civilization grew around independent coastal cities of the eastern Mediterranean, including Tyre, Sidon, Byblos, and Arwad. These communities were skilled seafarers and merchants rather than a single unified state. Their trade networks carried goods and cultural ideas around the Mediterranean, and Phoenician settlers established Carthage in North Africa. Famous products included timber from Lebanon and a valuable purple dye made from murex shells. Phoenician merchants also spread an alphabetic writing system that Greeks and Etruscans adapted. Alphabetic writing had earlier roots among West Semitic speakers, so the Phoenicians’ important role was in its use and diffusion, not its invention from nothing.

overview.text: The Paris Agreement is an international climate treaty adopted at a United Nations conference in Paris on 12 December 2015. It entered into force in 2016. Countries agreed to keep the rise in global average temperature well below 2°C above preindustrial levels and to pursue efforts toward a 1.5°C limit. Each country communicates its own climate plan, called a nationally determined contribution, describing actions on emissions and adaptation. The agreement uses a five-year cycle in which successive plans are expected to become more ambitious. It also addresses support for countries responding to climate change. The shared temperature goal guides national action but is not itself a guarantee that warming will stay below either threshold.

overview.text: War elephants were trained for battle in parts of ancient India and later appeared in Hellenistic and Carthaginian armies. Their size could frighten horses and troops, disrupt formations, and carry riders or fighting platforms. Alexander’s army encountered elephants at the Hydaspes in India, while Pyrrhus used them against Rome in Italy. Carthaginian forces also fielded elephants during the Punic Wars. Their power had limits: animals could panic or be wounded, and opponents learned ways to let them pass through prepared gaps. The history of war elephants connects several regions of the ancient world and shows how a striking weapon could be both valuable and unpredictable.

overview.text: Claudius ruled the Roman Empire from AD 41 to 54. During his reign, Roman forces invaded Britain in AD 43, and Claudius traveled there to receive the submission of part of the island. He also sponsored large public works, including an aqueduct, a harbor at Ostia, and an outlet intended to drain Lake Fucine. Ancient writer Suetonius describes a staged naval fight on the lake before the water was released. Such spectacles displayed imperial power to spectators as well as celebrating engineering works. Claudius is therefore linked both to the expansion of Roman rule in Britain and to the spectacular public events staged by emperors.

Roman forces invaded Britain in AD 43 under Claudius.
Claudius built an outlet for Lake Fucine and a harbor at Ostia.
